title: async/await under the hood
goal: Count the microtasks behind await and return, and predict where errors from async code end up.

steps.title: One await, one microtask
steps.text:
An async function runs synchronously until its first `await`; there control returns to the caller [[c:sync-until-await]]. `await x` first does `PromiseResolve(%Promise%, x)` [[c:await-promiseresolve]]: a native promise is used as is, anything else is wrapped. The rest of the function resumes in a promise reaction job once that promise is fulfilled.

On a native promise that is one microtask. It used to be three: V8 proposed the change, and it is now in the spec [[c:await-one-tick]]. Old blog posts and answers still show the three-tick orders.

Even `await null` yields: everything already in the microtask queue runs first [[c:await-always-yields]].

claims.text: Code before the first await runs synchronously; at await, control returns to the caller.

evidence.quote: Control exits the function and returns to the caller.

claims.text: Await converts its operand with PromiseResolve.
Using promiseResolve in await saved two microtask ticks when awaiting a promise.

evidence.quote: This way you save one of the additional promises, plus two ticks on the microtask queue, for the common case that the value passed to await is already a promise.
for each await the engine has to create two additional promises (even if the right hand side is already a promise) and it needs at least three microtask queue ticks.

claims.text: await yields even for a resolved promise or a non-promise.

evidence.quote: This happens even if the awaited value is an already-resolved promise or not a promise: execution doesn't return to the current function until all other already-scheduled microtasks are processed.

steps.title: Trace an await
steps: `f()` runs synchronously: logs `f1`, then calls `g()`, which also runs synchronously and logs `g`. `g` returns an already fulfilled native promise.
`await` on a native fulfilled promise queues one reaction job: resume `f`. Microtasks: [resume f]. `f()` returns its pending promise to the script.
`Promise.resolve().then(...)` queues its reaction at once. Microtasks: [resume f, p].
The script logs `s` and ends. The checkpoint runs `resume f` (logs `f2`), then `p`.
Output: `f1 g s f2 p`. With the old three-tick await, `p` would have come before `f2`.

steps.title: Thenables and returned promises cost more
steps.text:
The one-tick path needs a native promise. Awaiting a [thenable](g:thenable), such as a promise from another library, wraps it: resolving the wrapper with a thenable queues a job that calls its `then` [[c:thenable-job]], and only then the reaction. That is at least one extra tick, more if `then` settles later.

The same cost hides in `return p` from an async function: its own promise is resolved with `p`, so it pays that job, and `p.then` queues one more: two extra ticks. `return await p` pays one tick, then resolves with a plain value. MDN says `return await promise` is at least as fast as `return promise` [[c:return-await-fast]]. `new Promise((r) => r(p))` pays the two extra ticks as well; `Promise.resolve(p)` returns `p` itself.

Never build logic on tick counts. Expect them in interview puzzles.

claims.text: Resolving a promise with a thenable defers the chaining to a PromiseResolveThenableJob.

evidence.quote: This does deferred chaining of these promises on the next turn, expressed via what the specification calls a PromiseResolveThenableJob.
If it's called with a thenable value (including another Promise instance), then the thenable's then method is saved and called in the future (it's always called asynchronously).

claims.text: return await promise is at least as fast as return promise.

evidence.quote: Contrary to some popular belief, return await promise is at least as fast as return promise, due to how the spec and engines optimize the resolution of native promises.

steps.title: A method for ordering puzzles
steps.text:
For any mix of async functions, `then` chains and timers:

1. Run the script line by line. Log the synchronous output: async function bodies up to their first `await`, and promise executors.
2. Keep two lists: microtasks in queueing order, and tasks (timers by deadline).
3. Drain microtasks one by one. Each may append more: the next chain hop, the code after the next `await`.
4. Only when the list is empty, take one task, then drain again.

Most mistakes come from step 3. A hop is queued only when the previous handler runs. `await asyncFn()` costs extra ticks when `asyncFn` returns a promise, because its own promise is resolved with a thenable [[c:thenable-adopt]].

claims.text: A promise resolved with a thenable adopts the thenable's state.

evidence.quote: The promise may still be pending because it's resolved with another thenable, but its eventual state will match that of the resolved thenable.

steps.title: Errors: return vs return await, late handlers
steps.text:
`try/catch` sees a rejection only if it is awaited inside the `try`. `return p` leaves the block at once and hands `p` on, so its rejection skips the `catch`; `return await p` throws inside the `try` [[c:await-throws]]. A call neither awaited nor returned has no handler at all.

A rejection with no handler by the time microtasks have drained is reported. Browsers fire `unhandledrejection` [[c:browser-unhandled]]. Node's default mode `throw` turns it into an uncaught exception that ends the process [[c:node-unhandled-throw]]. A handler attached in a later task is too late [[c:late-handler]].

Classic trap: `await slow; await fast;` where `fast` rejects first. Nothing listens to `fast` yet [[c:sequential-await-unhandled]]. `Promise.all` attaches both handlers at once.

claims.text: await throws a rejection where it stands; a returned promise rejects after the function has returned.

evidence.quote: If the Promise is rejected, the rejected value is thrown.
the promise is rejected after it has already been returned from noAwait

claims.text: Browsers send unhandledrejection when a promise with no handler is rejected.

evidence.quote: The unhandledrejection event is sent to the global scope of a script when a JavaScript Promise that has no rejection handler is rejected; typically, this is the window, but may also be a Worker.

claims.text: Node's default throw mode raises an unhandled rejection as an uncaught exception.

evidence.quote: throw: Emit unhandledRejection. If this hook is not set, raise the unhandled rejection as an uncaught exception. This is the default.

claims.text: A handler attached after a turn of the event loop is late.

evidence.quote: The 'rejectionHandled' event is emitted whenever a Promise has been rejected and an error handler was attached to it (using promise.catch(), for example) later than one turn of the Node.js event loop.

claims.text: Sequential awaits can leave an early rejection unhandled.

evidence.quote: In sequentialWait, if promise fast rejects before promise slow is fulfilled, then an unhandled promise rejection error will be raised, regardless of whether the caller has configured a catch clause.

points: An async function runs synchronously to its first await; each await on a native promise costs one microtask (it used to be three).
await null and await 42 still yield to every microtask already queued.
`return p` from an async function and `new Promise(r => r(p))` cost two extra ticks, other thenables at least one; `return await p` is not slower.
try/catch only catches what is awaited inside the try: `return p` skips the catch.
A rejection with no handler when microtasks drain is reported; `await slow; await fast` leaves `fast` unhandled, Promise.all does not.

options.why: `await p` on a native fulfilled promise queues one reaction, before `a`'s. `b` is queued only when `a` runs.
That was the old three-tick await, from before the spec change. Awaiting a native promise now costs one tick, so its reaction is queued before `a`.
This is a two-tick await. `await p` uses `p` itself, so its reaction is queued first, right when the function suspends.
Each call runs to its first `await`, then returns. Each `await 0` costs one tick, so the two calls take turns.
`await 0` still yields, even for a non-promise. `f('b')` starts before `f('a')` resumes.
A resumed function does not keep running past its next `await`. Each `await` queues it behind the other call's continuation.
`t` is not a native promise, so it is wrapped. One job calls `t.then`, which fulfils the wrapper, then a second job resumes the function. `1` runs between them.
That is the order for a native promise. A plain thenable costs an extra tick: its `then` must be called in its own job first.
Awaiting a thenable is slower but not a task. Its jobs are microtasks and interleave with the chain.
`b` pays one tick for `await p`, then resolves with a plain value. `a` resolves its promise with `p`, a thenable, which costs extra ticks.
This assumes `return p` skips work by not awaiting. Resolving an async function's promise with a promise adds a thenable job.
Microtask order is fully specified. Only tasks that depend on outside timing can vary.
`Promise.resolve(p)` returns `p` itself, so `r` is queued at once. `r(p)` resolves with a thenable and pays two extra ticks.
Registration order is not queue order. The `new Promise` is still pending while the thenable job runs.
Resolving with a promise is legal: the new promise adopts its state. Both handlers run.

options.text: `A B C D G E F H`
options.why: Sync: A, B, C (g runs inside f), D (executor), G. Then microtasks: `f` resumes (E) before F, queued later. The timer task is last.

options.text: `A B C D G F E H`
options.why: This charges `await g()` extra ticks. `g` returns `undefined`, so its promise is a fulfilled native promise and the await costs one tick.

options.text: `A B D G C E F H`
options.why: An async function's body runs synchronously when called, so `g` logs C before `f` reaches its `await`.
`g` returns a promise, so its own promise is resolved with a thenable: two ticks. Then `await` costs one more, so `f` lands just before 3.
That holds if `g` returned a plain value. Returning a promise from an async function adds a thenable job and a reaction.
This counts only one extra tick. Adopting a thenable takes a job to call `then` and a job to run its reaction, before the await's own tick.
`fail()` returns a rejected promise; no exception is thrown in the `try`. `return` hands it on and `load()` rejects with `x`.
`catch` only sees a rejection that is awaited inside the `try`. `return fail()` returns before the rejection is unwrapped.
The caller passes a rejection handler to `then`, and `load()`'s promise adopts the rejection, so it is handled there.
Only `return await` unwraps the rejection inside the `try`, so only `b` falls back. `a` rejects with `x`.
This treats `return fail()` like `return await fail()`. Without `await` the rejection is never thrown inside the `try`.
`await` turns the rejection into a throw at that line, inside the `try`, so `b`'s `catch` runs.
`fail()` returns a rejected promise that nobody handles. `load` returns `ok`; after microtasks drain, Node reports the rejection.
An async function never throws synchronously to its caller. It returns a rejected promise, which `try` cannot see unless awaited.
The rejection is not lost. With no handler, Node reports it as unhandled, here through the listener.
`fast` rejects at 10 ms while the function still waits on `slow`, so no handler exists yet. At 20 ms `await fast` attaches one, too late.
`try` covers the `await fast` line, not the promise. Until that line runs, `fast` has no handler.
Node does not wait for the process to end. It checks for unhandled rejections each time the microtask queue drains, here right after the 10 ms timer.
`Promise.all` attaches handlers to both promises at once, so `fast`'s rejection is handled at 10 ms and fails the `all` early.
That is the sequential `await slow; await fast` case. `Promise.all` subscribes to `fast` before it rejects.
`Promise.all` rejects as soon as one input rejects, and the `await` inside `try` sees it.
